title: How to Deal With a Breakup: 10 Healthy Ways to Heal
h1: How to Deal With a Breakup: 10 Healthy Ways to Heal and Move Forward
description: Learn how to deal with a breakup in healthy ways: process your feelings, care for your body, limit rumination, lean on others and grow from the experience.
keyword: how to deal with a breakup
excerpt: Ten practical, compassionate ways to get through a breakup, from the first rough days to the lessons that help you love better next time.
intro:
A breakup can knock the wind out of you, even when you saw it coming and even when it was your choice. Suddenly the person you texted all day is gone, your routines feel off, and your mind keeps replaying the same scenes. That disorientation is normal. You lost something important, and grief is the natural response.

There's no shortcut through it, but there are ways to make the road gentler. This guide covers how to deal with a breakup in ways that actually help: expressing what you feel, looking after your body, quieting the obsessive thoughts, reconnecting with what you love, and eventually turning the experience into wisdom. Go at your own pace. Healing isn't a straight line, and some days will be better than others.
body:
Why breakups hurt so much

Romantic relationships weave themselves into everything: your daily routine, your plans for the future, your sense of who you are. When one ends, you're not only missing a person. You're also losing a set of habits, a future you'd imagined, and sometimes a shared friend group or home.

That's why a breakup can feel physical, with trouble sleeping, a knot in your stomach or no appetite. It's why you might cycle through sadness, anger, relief and longing in a single afternoon. None of this means you're doing it wrong. It means you cared.

Let your feelings out

1. Write it out or talk it out

Feelings that stay bottled up tend to grow louder. Giving them somewhere to go helps them settle.

  • Journal freely. Write for ten minutes without editing. What hurts most? What are you angry about? What do you miss?
  • Write an unsent letter. Say everything you wish you could say to your ex, then keep it or tear it up. The point is release, not delivery.
  • Talk to someone you trust. A good friend doesn't need to fix anything. They just need to listen.

If you notice the same painful thoughts looping for weeks, a licensed therapist can help you work through them with tools that friends usually can't offer.

Take care of your body first

2. Pay attention to your body

Emotional pain often shows up physically. Taking care of the basics gives your mind a steadier foundation.

  • Protect your sleep. Keep a regular bedtime, and put your phone across the room so you're not scrolling old photos at 2 a.m.
  • Eat regular meals. Even if your appetite is off, simple, nourishing food helps your energy and mood.
  • Go easy on alcohol. It can feel like relief in the moment but often makes sadness and sleep worse.
  • Get outside. Daylight and fresh air are small but real mood boosters.

3. Get active, but don't overdo it

Movement is one of the most reliable ways to ease stress. A brisk walk, a bike ride, a dance class or a yoga session can lift your mood and give you a break from your thoughts.

The catch is balance. Some people throw themselves into punishing workouts to avoid feeling anything. Aim for movement that feels good and restorative, not exhausting. If you're sore, sleeping badly or skipping rest days, dial it back.

Tip: Pair exercise with connection. Ask a friend to join you for a weekly walk or class. You'll get the mood boost of movement and the comfort of company at the same time.

Widen your focus beyond the breakup

4. Remind yourself of what's still good

When you're hurting, it's easy to feel like everything is falling apart. It usually isn't. Try a simple daily practice: write down three things that went okay or that you're grateful for. A friend who checked in. A good cup of coffee. A song that made you smile.

This isn't about pretending you're fine. It's about widening your view so the breakup isn't the only thing you see.

5. Do things you love (and try something new)

Relationships take up time, and many people let hobbies slip. Now is a great chance to reclaim them. Pick up the guitar again, return to the book club, or finally take that pottery class.

New experiences help too. Trying something unfamiliar builds a sense of identity that's yours alone, which is exactly what you need after a big loss. For more ideas, see our list of things to do to move on from a breakup.

Break the rumination cycle

6. Try an "obsession diet"

Rumination, the habit of going over the same thoughts again and again, can keep a breakup wound open for months. An obsession diet means deliberately limiting how much fuel you feed those thoughts.

  • Mute or unfollow your ex. You don't have to block them forever, but checking their profile keeps you hooked.
  • Put reminders away. Box up photos and gifts and store them out of sight.
  • Schedule "worry time." Give yourself fifteen minutes a day to think about the breakup. When thoughts pop up outside that window, note them and save them for later.
  • Redirect gently. When you catch yourself spiraling, switch to an activity that needs focus, like a puzzle, a game, cooking or a call with a friend.

If your ex is constantly on your mind, our guide on how to stop thinking about your ex has more strategies.

Stay connected to other people

7. Lean on your people

Breakups can make you want to hide. Resist that urge, at least a little. Reach out to friends and family, accept invitations even when you're not in the mood, and let people know what kind of support helps you. Some want distraction; others want to vent. Both are valid.

If your social circle overlapped heavily with your ex, it might be time to widen it. Our tips on making friends as an adult can help.

8. Give back to others

Helping someone else is a surprisingly powerful way to feel better. Volunteering, mentoring, helping a neighbor or supporting a friend through their own rough patch shifts your focus outward and reminds you that you have something valuable to offer.

It also adds structure to your week, which helps when your old routines have disappeared.

Look ahead without rushing

9. Resist the urge to rush back or rebound

In the first weeks, you might be tempted to text your ex at midnight or jump into something new to numb the pain. Both are understandable, and both tend to delay healing.

  • Before reaching out to your ex, ask: will this help me heal, or will it just give me a quick hit of relief?
  • Before dating again, ask: am I curious about meeting someone, or am I trying to fill a hole?

There's no fixed waiting period. You'll know you're ready when you can think about your ex without a strong pull either way.

Tip: If you find yourself reaching for your phone to contact your ex, text a friend instead. Agree in advance that they'll be your "call me first" person.

10. Learn the lessons the breakup can teach

Once the sharpest pain fades, a breakup or divorce can become a source of insight. Reflect without blaming yourself or your ex:

  • What did this relationship give you that you'd want again?
  • What needs of yours went unmet?
  • Were there early warning signs you noticed but brushed aside?
  • What would you do differently in how you communicated or handled conflict?

These answers become your guide for future relationships. They help you choose more wisely and show up as a better partner.

How long does it take to get over a breakup?

Everyone heals on their own timeline. The length of the relationship, how it ended, and what support you have all play a role. Some people feel noticeably better within a few weeks; for others, especially after a long relationship or divorce, it takes many months.

Progress often looks like this: the bad days get a bit less intense, the good days get a bit more frequent, and one day you realize you went hours without thinking about it. If you're struggling to function at work or at home, feel hopeless, or have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to a licensed mental health professional right away, or call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US.

The bottom line

Learning how to deal with a breakup is really about learning how to care for yourself through loss. Let yourself feel it, look after your body, limit the rumination, stay connected, and give yourself time. The pain is real, but so is your ability to heal. When you're ready for the next chapter, read how to move on after a break up or browse more breakup advice.
takeaways: Breakup pain is real grief; sadness, anger and relief can all show up at once.
Express your feelings through journaling, unsent letters or talking with someone you trust.
Protect sleep, food and gentle exercise to steady your mood.
Limit rumination by muting your ex, storing reminders and scheduling worry time.
Reflect on lessons once the sharpest pain fades, and seek professional help if you're struggling to cope.

faq.q: What is the healthiest way to deal with a breakup?
faq.a: Let yourself feel the loss, talk to supportive people, keep up basic routines like sleep, meals and movement, and limit contact with your ex and their social media. Over time, reflect on what you learned. If sadness lingers or overwhelms daily life, consider a licensed therapist.

faq.q: How long does it take to get over a breakup?
faq.a: It varies widely. Shorter relationships may take a few weeks to recover from, while long relationships or divorces can take many months. Healing tends to come gradually, with bad days becoming less intense and good days more frequent. Be patient with your own pace.

faq.q: Should I stay friends with my ex after a breakup?
faq.a: Friendship can work for some people, but usually only after a period of no contact and once romantic feelings have faded. If staying in touch keeps you hoping, hurting or checking their life, it's healthier to create distance first. Your healing comes first.

faq.q: Why can't I stop thinking about my ex?
faq.a: Your brain is adjusting to the loss of someone who was part of your daily life, so repeated thoughts are common. Muting their social media, putting away reminders, scheduling limited worry time and redirecting to absorbing activities can gradually reduce rumination.
